opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about it in a few phases. The first was almost accidental. Once ChatGPT launched, a large number of people started using it for health questions: understanding a lab result, preparing for a doctor's appointment, figuring out whether a symptom was worth worrying about. Health quickly became one of the most common things people came to the product for. So before we had a dedicated effort, we already had a big responsibility, because people were relying on these models for something that really matters in their lives.

The second phase was taking that seriously as a research and safety problem. If people are going to ask these questions, the model needs to be good at answering them. That means accurate, but also knowing when to hedge, when to ask a follow-up question, when to say "you should really see someone about this today." Much of the early work was about measurement. We needed ways to evaluate health conversations that reflect how people actually use the product, rather than multiple-choice medical exam questions, which the models had largely saturated. We worked with a lot of physicians to define what a good response looks like across many realistic scenarios, and that became the target we trained against.

The third phase, which we're in now, is moving from "the model answers health questions well" to "the model actually helps improve health outcomes." That's a much harder bar. It means thinking about the whole experience: grounding answers in a person's own context when they choose to share it, helping clinicians with their workflows, and partnering with health systems so these tools reach people where care actually happens. It also means being humble about what we don't know yet. A model scoring well on an eval doesn't by itself prove it makes people healthier, so we're increasingly interested in real-world evidence.

The through-line across all of it is that we see health as one of the clearest cases where AI can be broadly beneficial. Many people around the world don't have easy access to a doctor, or they get ten rushed minutes and leave confused. If we can give everyone something like a knowledgeable, careful, always-available companion for their health, and do it responsibly, that's a large impact. But the responsibility part has to scale along with the capability, and that's what keeps the work interesting.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes growing adoption first, then safety research, then impact. It does not present the specified progression from a safety foundation through growing adoption to scaling impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that there have really been a few distinct phases, and each one was kind of unlocked by the one before it.

The first phase, honestly, wasn't something we designed. It was people just showing up and using ChatGPT for health. Pretty early on we noticed that a meaningful fraction of conversations were about health in some way: someone trying to understand a lab result, someone deciding whether a symptom was worth a trip to urgent care, caregivers trying to figure out what questions to ask at their parent's next appointment. That was happening organically, at a scale that I don't think any health system or telehealth company has ever operated at. So the first realization was less "we should build a health product" and more "we already have one, whether we like it or not, and we have a responsibility to make it good."

That led into the second phase, which was really about measurement. If people are going to rely on these models for health information, you need to know where they're actually good and where they fall down. And the existing benchmarks were mostly exam-style, multiple choice, medical licensing questions. Those are fine as a sanity check, but they tell you almost nothing about whether a model handles a messy, real conversation well: does it ask the right follow-up, does it recognize when something is an emergency, does it communicate uncertainty, does it know when to say "go see someone." So we put a lot of work into building evaluations that were grounded in how physicians actually judge quality, with a lot of clinicians involved in defining what good looks like across many specialties and languages. That was a big investment, and I think it was the right one, because you can't improve what you can't see.

The third phase is where it gets more interesting, which is actually using those evaluations to make the models better and then shipping that in ways that are more intentional. Once you can measure things like safety behavior, calibration, communication quality, you can train against them, and you start to see real gains that aren't just "the model got smarter in general." And then on the product side, you start thinking about what it means to actually be useful in someone's health journey over time, rather than just answering a one-off question. Things like being able to bring in your own records, continuity across conversations, being more helpful on the follow-through side.

And then I think the phase we're entering now is about the clinician side and the system side. Most of the attention has been on consumers, but a huge amount of the value, and frankly a lot of the risk, sits in how these tools get used by doctors, nurses, administrators, researchers. The documentation burden, the time clinicians spend fighting the EHR, the back-office work, that's all stuff where the models are already quite capable and the question is more about deployment, trust, and integration.

So if I zoom out: it started with users pulling us into health, we responded by getting serious about measurement, measurement let us actually improve the models and build real products, and now we're trying to work across the whole system rather than just the patient-facing piece. The through-line for me has always been that the opportunity is enormous, access to good health information is wildly unevenly distributed, but the bar for getting it right is also really high, and you earn the right to do the ambitious stuff by being rigorous about the basics first.

r001.rationale: The response describes a progression from organic user adoption to measurement, model and product improvements, and broader clinician/system deployment. It does not frame the progression as starting with a safety foundation before growing adoption.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as a progression from capability to usefulness. Early on, the question is: can these models understand medical information and reason about it? That’s an important foundation, but answering a medical question correctly isn’t the same as helping someone in a real health context.

The next step is understanding what happens when the model has incomplete information, when it needs to ask a follow-up question, or when it should express uncertainty. And then there’s the question of how it fits into someone’s life or a clinician’s workflow. Can it help a person understand their care? Can it reduce the work that gets in the way of a clinician spending time with a patient?

So I wouldn’t describe progress purely in terms of better benchmark scores. The thing we ultimately want to understand is whether these systems can be useful and reliable in practice. That requires careful evaluation and learning from the people who would actually use them.

r001.rationale: The response describes a progression from medical capability toward practical usefulness and reliability, but does not frame it as moving from a safety foundation through growing adoption to scaled impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it as a progression from general capability toward something people can reliably use in a health context. As models get better at reasoning, understanding images, and working with information, they become more useful for health questions. But being able to answer a medical question is only one part of building something useful.

You also need to understand the context, recognize when information is missing, communicate uncertainty, and know when someone needs help from a clinician. And you need to evaluate those behaviors with people who actually practice medicine.

So the direction is toward helping people understand their health and helping clinicians do their work, with increasingly rigorous evidence about where these systems are useful and where their limitations are. I wouldn’t think of that as one moment when a model suddenly becomes a doctor. It’s a series of specific uses that we have to earn confidence in.

r001.rationale: The response describes progress from general model capability toward health use and stronger evidence, but it does not communicate the sequence of establishing a safety foundation, growing adoption, and then scaling impact.
